claims.text: Elemental distribution governs the reliable formation and catalytic performance of noble metal-based high-entropy alloy nanomaterials.
Lattice strain governs the reliable formation and catalytic performance of noble metal-based high-entropy alloy nanomaterials.
Surface segregation governs the reliable formation and catalytic performance of noble metal-based high-entropy alloy nanomaterials.
The combined effects of elemental distribution, lattice strain, and surface segregation are synergistic.
In situ characterization, DFT simulations, and machine-learning algorithms can optimize elemental distribution, lattice strain, surface segregation, material formation, and catalytic performance.
The target noble metal-based high-entropy alloy nanomaterials have a uniform elemental distribution.
The target noble metal-based high-entropy alloy nanomaterials have an FCC crystal structure.
The combined effects of elemental distribution, lattice strain, and surface segregation produce a stable catalytic surface.
The combined effects of elemental distribution, lattice strain, and surface segregation produce an active catalytic surface.
Formation of a stable and active catalytic surface enhances catalytic performance.
The proposed approach will increase catalytic activity by 20–30% relative to traditional noble metal catalysts such as Pt/C or Pd/C.
The proposed approach will improve material stability by 10–20% relative to traditional noble metal catalysts such as Pt/C or Pd/C.

The proposed mechanism is expected to hold for uniformly distributed, FCC noble metal-based high-entropy alloy nanomaterials under catalytic conditions of 300–500 K, 1–10 atm, and 1–10 mM reactant concentration.
DFT and machine-learning prediction errors, as well as unspecified additional factors, may affect material formation and catalytic performance.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome uses traditional Pt/C or Pd/C catalysts as the baseline, whereas the controlled experiment compares high-entropy alloys made using the combined approach with high-entropy alloys made using traditional synthesis methods. These are different control comparisons.

The rule describes a result as 'not significantly improved' while specifying p < 0.05, which ordinarily denotes statistical significance. The direction of the statistical criterion is therefore internally inconsistent.
